 Cybersecurity expert sounds alarm over US infrastructure vulnerabilities amid widespread outages
 Dr Ram Dantu said recent disruptions may reveal vulnerabilities in electric grids, water systems and telecommunications

 By Michael Sinkewicz , Brooke Taylor FOXBusiness close video Cybersecurity expert warns aging US infrastructure could expose critical systems to attacks 
 University of North Texas cybersecurity expert Dr. Ram Dantu warns that recent technology outages could expose vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure, while cautioning that potential cyberattacks cannot yet be ruled out.
 A leading cybersecurity expert warned that a recent wave of technology outages across the United States could expose vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure, raising concerns that foreign adversaries may exploit weaknesses in the nation's most essential systems.
 Dr. Ram Dantu, founding director of the University of North Texas' Center for Cyber and AI Security and a former Cisco director, told Fox News national correspondent Brooke Taylor that a string of technology and aviation outages in recent days could be attributed to network congestion or software problems.
 However, he said cybersecurity threats should not be dismissed and warrant thorough investigation.
 "Nobody can guarantee this is not a cyberattack," Dantu said.
 JAY CLAYTON ADDRESSES CONCERNS AMID WIDESPREAD TECH OUTAGES 
 A bank branch is experiencing disruptions due to a banking technology outage. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital) 
 He warned that malicious software can remain hidden or dormant in computer networks for extended periods, allowing it to spread gradually before being activated remotely.
 "If there is a foreign actor, they will keep quiet for a long period of time, and then slowly they will release, and remotely they will be activated," Dantu said.
 Dantu expressed particular concern about the potential consequences of cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure , including electric grids, water systems, telecommunications networks and financial institutions.
 "Cyberattack can be massive on real critical infrastructure," he said. "Electric grid, water grid, oil and natural gas and telecommunications. These are very, very critical systems."
 JPMORGAN CHASE SYSTEMS RECOVERING FOLLOWING HOURSLONG NATIONWIDE TECHNICAL OUTAGE 
 The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop Friday after radar and communications systems experienced instability, disrupting thousands of flights. (Robyn Stevens Brody/Sipa USA / Reuters) 
 Dantu's warning follows days of disruptions affecting numerous facets of American society, including financial institutions, online services and U.S. national security infrastructure.
 Major tech companies , including Microsoft, have faced widespread outages, while a nationwide ground stop imposed by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday delayed and canceled thousands of flights, stranding hundreds of thousands of travelers.
 Dantu warned that the wave of outages could provide adversaries with clues about vulnerabilities in critical U.S. systems.
 "My worry also is that all these pointers will help the adversaries ... to plan their action," he said. "I think we are showing our weakness, and I am really concerned about it."
 Dantu also questioned the timing of major system upgrades, calling daytime installations unusual and noting that engineers typically schedule updates overnight and in stages.
 FAA PAUSES ROUTER INSTALLATIONS NATIONWIDE AFTER TECH ISSUE CAUSED FRIDAY'S GROUND STOP 
 Secretary of State Marco Rubio said federal officials found no evidence linking recent technology outages to one another or to foreign hackers and other malicious actors. (Carlos Barria/Reuters / Reuters) 
 "They do it in the middle of the night. These upgrades, they don't do in the day, 12 o'clock or one o'clock in the afternoon. No, that's very rare," he said. "They don't do it in the middle of the day. I think that is strange. That's what caught my eye."
 Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that federal officials had found no evidence linking the recent technology disruptions to one another or to foreign adversaries.
 "We have zero evidence whatsoever. We have no indication, no evidence, and no reason to believe at all that any of these incidents are related to each other," Rubio told reporters.
 He also said officials had found no evidence suggesting the outages were caused by hackers, criminal groups or foreign governments.

 Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also said officials had found no signs of a coordinated cyberattack, instead pointing to security patches and system upgrades as possible explanations for the disruptions.
 FOX Business' Brittany Miller contributed to this report.
